entry: Tropical plant, *Colocasia esculenta*, of the family [[Araceae]], grown for its starchy corm, a root [[Vegetable|vegetable]]. Taro is the most widely cultivated of several Araceae species whose corms, leaves, stems and petioles are eaten. Its corms are a food staple in African, Caribbean, Oceanian, East Asian, Southeast Asian and South Asian cultures, similar to yams. The plant is thought to have originated in the Indomalayan realm, perhaps in East India, Nepal and Bangladesh, and spread through cultivation to Southeast Asia, East Asia, the Pacific Islands, Egypt, Africa, the Caribbean and the Americas. The English name was borrowed from Māori after Captain Cook observed plantations in New Zealand in 1769. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] described two species, but many later botanists consider them a single, very variable species.

Set of playing cards used in [[Card game|card games]] and for fortune-telling or [[Divination|divination]]. From at least the mid-15th century, tarot was used to play trick-taking games such as Tarocchini. The cards were first known as *trionfi* and later as *tarocchi*. From their [[Italy|Italian]] roots, tarot games spread across most of Europe, evolving into forms such as German Grosstarock and French Tarot, now the second most popular card game in France. Divinatory use began in late 18th-century France, when occultists made elaborate but unsubstantiated claims about the cards' history and meaning. Tarot packs have four suits that vary by region, each with 14 cards, plus a separate 21-card trump suit and a single card known as the Fool.

Small nocturnal [[Primate|primate]] of the family Tarsiidae, the only living family in its infraorder. Extant tarsiers are native to Maritime Southeast Asia, predominantly in [[Brunei]], [[Indonesia]], [[Malaysia]] and the [[Philippines]], where they live mainly in forests, especially those with lianas, which give vertical support for climbing. Fossils from [[China]], [[Thailand]] and Pakistan show the group was once more widespread. Tarsiers have large eyes and elongated tarsal bones in the hind limbs, and can leap more than 45 times their body length. Their diet consists mainly of arthropods such as insects and spiders. Taxonomists debated their place among primates through much of the 20th century, and in 2010 two researchers proposed splitting the genus *Tarsius* into three genera. About 14 species are recognized, many of them threatened by habitat destruction.

Comedy in verse by [[Molière]], first performed in 1664. The play [[Satire|satirizes]] religious hypocrisy through Tartuffe, a fraud who feigns devotion to win control of the household and property of Orgon, a bourgeois head of household. After a performance at [[Palace of Versailles|Versailles]] that year, King [[Louis XIV]] suppressed the play, probably under the influence of the Archbishop of Paris. The text of that first version has been lost. The play was revised in 1667 to be less provocative and re-released in its current form in 1669. It is written in twelve-syllable rhyming couplets (alexandrines), 1,962 lines in all. In French and English alike, "tartuffe" now designates a hypocrite who feigns virtue, especially religious virtue.

Capital and largest city of [[Uzbekistan]] and the most populous city in [[Central Asia]] (pop., 2025: more than 3.1 million). The city grew as a trading center on the [[Silk Road]]. Before the influence of [[Islam]] in the mid-8th century AD, Sogdian and Turkic culture predominated. After [[Genghis Khan]] destroyed the city in 1219, it was rebuilt. For much of the 18th and 19th centuries it was an independent city-state, before the Khanate of Kokand conquered it. In 1865 it fell to the [[Russian Empire]] and became capital of Russian Turkestan. Soviet-era growth brought major demographic change, including forced deportations from across the Soviet Union. After the 1966 Tashkent earthquake destroyed much of the city, it was rebuilt as a model Soviet city. In the first half of 2024 Tashkent accounted for 19% of Uzbekistan's GDP, and a 2023 report ranked it first among the country's regions.

Marginal sea of the South Pacific Ocean between [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. Named after the Dutch explorer Abel Janszoon Tasman, who in 1642 was the first known European to cross it, the sea was extensively navigated in the 1770s by [[James Cook|Lieutenant James Cook]] during his three voyages of exploration. It is about 2,800 km (1,700 mi) from north to south, with an area of 2,300,000 sq km (890,000 sq mi) and a maximum depth of 5,943 m (19,498 ft). Its midocean ridge developed 85 to 55 million years ago as [[Zealandia]] and Australia broke apart during the breakup of the supercontinent [[Gondwana]]. The [[Māori people|Māori]] call the sea Te Moana-a-Rehua, meaning "the sea of Rehua". Lord Howe Island and Ball's Pyramid are among its midsea islands.

Island state of [[Australia]], south of the mainland across [[Bass Strait]] (pop., 2023: 573,479). It includes the main island of Tasmania, the 26th-largest island in the world, and more than 1,000 smaller islands. The capital and largest city, [[Hobart]], holds about 40% of the population. Europeans permanently settled the island in 1803 as a penal colony of the [[British Empire]]. Violent conflict known as the Black War peaked between 1825 and 1831 and, with disease, sharply reduced the Aboriginal population. About 80,000 convicts were sent to Van Diemen's Land, the colony's earlier name, before transportation ended in 1853. The colony was renamed Tasmania in 1856, honoring the Dutch explorer [[Abel Tasman]]. The island federated as one of six founding states of Australia in 1901. About 42% of its land is protected in reserves, and the first environmental political party in the world was founded there.

Stocky carnivorous [[Marsupial|marsupial]] of the family Dasyuridae, now confined to the Australian island of [[Tasmania]]. It was formerly present on mainland Australia but became extinct there about 3,500 years ago. After the [[Thylacine|thylacine]] went extinct in 1936, it became the largest carnivorous marsupial in the world. Its large head and neck allow one of the strongest bites per unit body mass of any living predatory land mammal. Devils are usually solitary but sometimes eat together, and they can climb trees and swim across rivers. Females give birth to 20 to 30 live young after three weeks' gestation, but with only four nipples in the pouch, few newborns survive. Devil facial tumor disease has drastically reduced the population since the late 1990s, and the species was declared endangered in 2008. The animal is an iconic symbol of Tasmania and became known worldwide through the [[Looney Tunes]] character of the same name.

Sandstone plateau in the [[Sahara]] of southeastern [[Algeria]], its name meaning "plateau of rivers". It covers more than 72,000 sq km (28,000 sq mi) and holds one of the world's most important groupings of prehistoric [[Rock art|rock art]]. Its rock forests of eroded sandstone resemble a lunar landscape, and nearly 300 natural rock arches have formed in the southeast. The highest point, Adrar Afao, rises to 2,158 m (7,080 ft). Silurian and Devonian rock layers in the area yield petroleum and natural gas, extracted in the Illizi Basin to the north. The site is a national park and a Biosphere Reserve, and was inscribed as a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1982.

Chemical sense detected mainly by taste buds on the [[Tongue|tongue]]. Taste combines with smell and texture to determine the flavor of food. Each taste bud contains 50 to 100 taste receptor cells. The five basic tastes are sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness and savoriness, the last also known by its Japanese name [[Umami|umami]], meaning "deliciousness". Sweetness, savoriness and bitterness are detected when molecules bind to G protein-coupled receptors, while saltiness and sourness come from [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] and [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] ions. Sweetness identifies energy-rich foods, while bitterness warns of poisons. Taste perception fades with age, as papillae are lost and saliva production declines. [[Cat|Cats]] cannot taste sweetness, and some rodents can taste [[Starch|starch]], which humans cannot.

Indian multinational conglomerate headquartered in [[Mumbai]], established in 1868. It is India's largest conglomerate. Tata Sons is the holding company and promoter of more than 20 publicly listed affiliates, with a combined market capitalization of ₹31.17 trillion (US$330 billion) as of October 2025. The Tata Iron and Steel Company, now [[Steel|Tata Steel]], was established in 1907. The group's airline, founded in 1932, became [[Air India]]. The Taj Mahal Hotel opened in 1903 as the first hotel with electricity in British India.

Turkic-speaking peoples of Eastern Europe and northern Asia. The ethnonym probably first referred to a Tatar confederation, which was incorporated into the [[Mongol Empire]] when [[Genghis Khan]] unified the steppe tribes. Western cartographers later applied the name to peoples across Tartary, a region falsely conflated with the Mongol Empire. The largest, the Volga Tatars, live in the Volga-Ural region of European Russia and make up 53% of the population of [[Tatarstan]]. An estimated 5.3 million ethnic Tatars lived in Russia as of 2010. Genetic studies indicate that the Volga, Crimean and Siberian groups are apparently unrelated, with independent origins.

Republic of [[Russia]] in [[Eastern Europe]], in the Volga Federal District, with its capital and largest city at [[Kazan]]. It covers 68,000 sq km (26,000 sq mi), and its population was 4,004,809 at the 2021 census. Ethnic Tatars form about 53% of the population. The main source of wealth is [[Oil|oil]], supporting a strong petrochemical industry, with estimated deposits of over one billion tons. The earliest known organized state within its boundaries was [[Volga Bulgaria]], which adopted [[Islam]] in 922. Later predecessors included the [[Golden Horde]] and the [[Khanate of Kazan]] before Russian conquest. The Tatar ASSR, an autonomous republic of the Russian SFSR, was founded in 1920 and renamed the Republic of Tatarstan in 1992. Tatar and Russian are its official languages.

Design made by inserting ink, [[Dye|dyes]] or [[Pigment|pigments]] into the dermis, a form of [[Body modification|body modification]]. Tattooing dates to [[Neolithic]] times, and the first known tattooed person, Ötzi, lived around 3330 BC. Tattoos may be decorative, symbolic, pictorial or textual. Many have marked rites of passage, status, religious devotion, bravery, fertility or love, while others have marked outcasts, slaves and convicts. In the 20th century, tattooing in much of the world was associated with sailors and prisoners. In the 21st century, people choose tattoos for artistic, cosmetic, memorial, religious or spiritual reasons, or to show belonging to a group. The English word derives from the Samoan *tatau*, meaning "to strike". Tattoos are also used for identification, permanent makeup and medical purposes.

Single star in the constellation Cetus, similar to the [[Sun]] but with about 78% of its mass. It is the closest solitary G-type star, just under 12 light-years (3.7 parsecs) from the [[Solar System]]. The star is stable and low in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Observations detected more than ten times as much surrounding dust as in the Solar System, and no unambiguous planets had been confirmed as of 2025. Tau Ceti is consistently listed as a target for the [[Search for extraterrestrial intelligence|search for extraterrestrial intelligence]].

Elementary [[Lepton|lepton]] similar to the [[Electron|electron]] but much heavier, with negative electric charge. Its corresponding [[Antiparticle|antiparticle]] is the antitau. Its mass is 1776.9 MeV/c², compared with 105.66 MeV/c² for the [[Muon|muon]] and 0.511 MeV/c² for the electron. Its lifetime is 2.9×10⁻¹³ s. It is the only lepton with enough mass to decay into [[Hadron|hadrons]]. Its partner is the [[Neutrino|tau neutrino]]. Tau particles were detected between 1974 and 1977 at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center through anomalous collision events, and Martin Lewis Perl, whose group made the detection, shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics. The symbol τ comes from the Greek word for "third", as it was the third charged lepton discovered.

Naturally occurring organic compound, an amino sulfonic acid widely distributed in mammalian tissues. Although usually classed as an [[Amino acid|amino acid]], it is not incorporated into proteins. It is a major constituent of bile and is found in the [[Large intestine|large intestine]]. Taurine was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by German scientists Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin, and its name comes from the Latin *taurus*, meaning bull or ox. It is abundant in human organs but not an essential nutrient. Taurine is sold as a [[Dietary supplement|dietary supplement]] and used as a food additive for cats.

Zodiac constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere, depicting a bull. It dates back at least to the Early Bronze Age, when it marked the Sun's position at the spring equinox. The red giant [[Aldebaran]] is its brightest star. It contains two of the nearest open clusters to Earth, the [[Pleiades]] and the [[Hyades (star cluster)|Hyades]]. The [[Crab Nebula]], a supernova remnant, lies in its northeast part. Taurus is the only constellation crossed by the galactic equator, the celestial equator and the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]].

Vehicle for hire that provides point-to-point transportation for passengers, typically on an exclusive, non-shared basis. Regulation, hiring and payment methods differ between countries. Hackney carriages are licensed for street hailing, private hire vehicles (minicabs) for pre-booking only, and [[Limousine|limousines]] also for pre-booking. Taxibuses, such as jitneys and jeepneys in developing countries, run set routes with multiple stops. Unlike [[Public transport|public transport]], taxis carry individual passengers. Paris taxicabs were first fitted with meters in 1898, and [[London]]'s first hackney-carriage licenses were issued in 1662. Affordable [[Car|automobiles]] made motorized taxis common in the early 1900s. Ridesharing apps offer similar service but are usually regulated separately.

1976 American neo-noir film directed by [[Martin Scorsese]]. [[Robert De Niro|Robert De Niro]] plays Travis Bickle, a [[Vietnam War|Vietnam War]] veteran who works nights as a taxi driver in [[New York City]] and becomes a vigilante. The 12-year-old [[Jodie Foster]] plays a child prostitute, and the film's graphic violence drew controversy. It won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival|1976 Cannes Film Festival]] and received four Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture. It was said to have inspired John Hinckley Jr.'s attempted assassination of President [[Ronald Reagan]] in 1981. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 1994.

Art of preserving an animal's body by mounting or stuffing it for display or study. It is practiced mainly on [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], and the word derives from Greek words meaning "arrangement of skin". Taxidermy is used for hunting trophies, natural history displays and study skins of extinct or threatened species, and to memorialize pets. Unlike meat harvesting, it does not require killing an animal that could otherwise have lived. In [[Tenochtitlan]], capital of the [[Aztec Empire]], taxidermized eagles had deep ritual significance. In an 1803–1804 article, Louis Dufresne, a taxidermist at France's Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle, made known Jean-Baptiste Bécœur's method using [[Arsenic|arsenical]] soap, which let the [[Museum|museum]] build an immense bird collection. Nineteenth-century hunters' trophies were sewn and stuffed with rags, and the term "stuffing" evolved from that crude practice. Professional taxidermists prefer "mounting".

Level at which a group of organisms, a taxon or clade, is placed in a hierarchical system of classification. The most inclusive groups, such as Eukarya and Animalia, receive the highest ranks, and the least inclusive, such as *Homo sapiens*, the lowest. Ranks are either absolute, drawn from predefined terms such as [[Kingdom (taxonomy)|kingdom]], [[Genus|genus]] and [[Species|species]], or relative, shown by indentation. Rank-based codes such as the Zoological Code require absolute ranks. The [[Red fox|red fox]], *Vulpes vulpes*, belongs to the family [[Canidae]] and the order [[Carnivora]].

Practice and science of classification, developing an underlying scheme of classes and allocating things to them. Originally applied only to organisms grouped by shared characteristics, the term now covers things and concepts, such as library classification systems and search-engine taxonomies. Taxonomies rest on empirical and objective characteristics, unlike typologies, which rely on abstract or subjective criteria. The units of a taxonomy, called taxa, are often arranged as hierarchies, with a root node that applies to all objects. The word was coined in 1813 by the Swiss botanist A. P. de Candolle.

[[Conifer|Coniferous]] tree of the family Taxaceae, known as the European yew. Native to much of Europe, parts of West Asia, the [[Caucasus]] and northwest Africa, it is a woodland tree. All parts except the fleshy aril are poisonous. Its wood was prized for longbows and for musical instruments such as lutes. Yews are often planted in churchyards, where some reach great age. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] described it in 1753, and the name has 108 synonyms. Extracts from its bark and needles yield paclitaxel, a [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] drug.

American singer-songwriter known for autobiographical songwriting and frequent artistic reinvention. Swift began as a [[Country music|country]] singer with *Taylor Swift* (2006) and *Fearless* (2008), then moved to pop with *1989* (2014). After moving to Republic Records in 2018, she re-recorded four of her first six albums following a dispute with Big Machine. Her later albums include the indie folk *Folklore* and *Evermore* (both 2020). The Eras Tour (2023–2024) is the highest-grossing concert tour of all time. Swift is the highest-grossing live music artist and one of the best-selling music artists of all time. She has won 14 [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], including a record four Album of the Year wins, and was named [[Time (magazine)|Time]] Person of the Year in 2023, the first individual from the arts so honored. Her fans are known as Swifties.
